segments.text: Verse 2
Allah, the Eternal Refuge[1].
Once you know that Allah is One, to whom do you bring your needs? The answer follows:
Allah, the Eternal Refuge[1].
He is the One to whom people turn for refuge and bring their needs.

The name Allah is stated again, rather than replaced with the pronoun “He.” His name is thus repeated on the tongue, the heart recalls Him, and the worshiper seeks blessing by remembering Him. The Samad to whom you turn is Allah, whose unique oneness you have come to know.

Several explanations have been given for al-Samad, and the name should not be reduced to just one of them. One is that He has no interior cavity and neither eats nor drinks. This expresses His freedom from the needs of created beings, as He says:
Who feeds but is not fed
A human being needs food and drink, with one need following another: scarcely is one met before another arises. Allah, however, needs no one.

Another explanation is that He is perfect in His attributes. Ibn ‘Abbas is reported to have explained it as the Master whose mastery is perfect, the Forbearing whose forbearance is perfect, the Self-Sufficient whose self-sufficiency is perfect, the All-Knowing whose knowledge is perfect, and the Wise whose wisdom is perfect.
It has also been explained as the Master to whom creation turns with its needs.

The connection between these meanings becomes clear: they turn to Him because He is self-sufficient and they are in need, and because His knowledge, power, and mercy are perfect—not because He needs someone to help Him meet their needs.
He is not one of several counterparts with differing abilities. He is the One without equal, the Samad to whom perfection belongs.
When people cannot solve a problem, they ordinarily look for someone who can, seeking out the most capable person within reach.

How, then, can someone know his Lord’s perfection yet attach his heart to someone who cannot himself do without Him? Al-Samad is the One before whom you lay your needs, turning to Him with all the neediness and hope in your heart, whether you possess some means of meeting those needs or can find none.
This is not asking with the tongue while the heart remains turned elsewhere. It is a real attachment to the One you ask.
To illustrate the longing and need in this attachment, some linguistic discussions cite an expression meaning
the weaned camel calf yearned for its mother
. The calf in this illustration has been weaned; when separated from its mother, it longs intensely for her, crying out as if to complain that it cannot bear being away from her.
It has been suggested that this meaning is connected to the derivation of the name Allah. This is a reported view, not an etymology asserted with certainty.

The image is intended to help us understand the yearning heart, without likening Allah to His creation. Just as love for a mother differs from love for a friend or a child, the heart has a devotion, love, and need that can rightly be directed only to Allah.

Sincere devotion includes recognizing these feelings within yourself, nourishing them by remembering your Lord, and directing them to Him, rather than allowing created beings and practical means to take them over.
You see this reliance in the story of Moses’ mother, when she was commanded:
when you fear for him, cast him into the river

She feared for her son, yet his safety lay in obeying Allah’s command, even though the water appeared to be a place of danger. What mattered here was her trust in the One who commanded her and gave her His promise, rather than the outward appearance of the path alone.
You see a similar certainty in Hud’s stand before his people. He said:
So plot against me all together, then give me no respite.
He then explained what he relied on:
I put my trust in Allah, my Lord and your Lord.
He concluded with
My Lord is on a straight path[2].
He knew his Lord’s power and trusted His justice and governance. One of His names is al-Mu’min, and His servant is secure in knowing that his Lord will neither wrong him nor break His promise.
He therefore did not weigh his own strength against his people’s while forgetting the One who held everyone’s affairs in His hands.
This is why knowing Allah’s oneness is connected with security, as in His words:
Those who believe and do not mix their faith with falsehood[1] are the ones who will be secure, and it is they who are rightly guided.

Just as you turn to Allah with your needs, you turn to His revelation to learn what pleases Him and what He commands. Turning to Him does not mean asking for His gifts and then living as though you could do without His guidance.
None of this conflicts with using practical means; Allah Himself has made them part of how life works.

Someone who wants a harvest tills the soil, plants the seed, and waters and tends it. Leaving the field unplanted and asking for a harvest to fall from the sky is not the ordinary path Allah has established.
Someone who is ill looks for medicine and seeks treatment. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said,
There is no disease that Allah has created, except that He also has created its treatment.
Yet even while seeking treatment, the sick person remembers that healing comes from Allah, joining effort with the prayer
heal the patient, for You are the Healer. No healing is of any avail but Yours
Likewise, a person works for a living without treating work as an independent provider, and takes the means to victory while remaining certain that
victory only comes from Allah
The problem lies not in using a means, but in forgetting its Lord until fear and hope become attached to the instrument alone.

Means may produce results, fail to do so, or lead to something quite different from what was expected. If someone’s heart was attached to Allah from the outset, his connection with Him will not be severed when one of his means fails.
Beyond the adornments of the earth that absorb our attention, the truth remains that Allah governs all affairs. He is
the First[1] and the Last[2]
: no means begins independently of Him, and no outcome passes into a dominion beyond His.

Careful preparation and complete reliance came together in the migration to Madinah. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, arranged the route, guidance, and provisions. Yet the pursuers came so close to the cave that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said that if one of them looked beneath his feet, he would see them.
The Prophet’s reply was not a list of the precautions they had taken. He said,
O Abu Bakr! What do you think of two (persons) the third of whom is Allah?
The Quran also records what he told his companion:
Do not grieve; Allah is with us.
Trust in Allah had not begun only once their resources were exhausted. It was with him before he took action, as he acted, and when danger intensified.
Miracles, too, show that familiar means do not constrain Allah’s power: a staff becomes a snake, the sea parts, and Jesus brings the dead to life by Allah’s permission.
These signs free people from the illusion that what they are used to is all that is possible.

A believer does not make faith conditional on witnessing something extraordinary in every ordeal. The Quran has come to him as revelation to guide him and as a sign of the truth of the message. From it he learns belief in the unseen, a quality of those who are guided described at the beginning of Al-Baqarah:
those who believe in the unseen
His heart should not lose its way among the branching paths of practical means and forget the One to whom all affairs return.
Changing worldly circumstances reveal the difference between attachment to Allah and attachment to His gifts.
Allah says of some people:
There are some people who worship Allah on the edge [of faith][1]: if something good comes to them, they are content
. Such a person is reassured by the worldly good he receives, and when it disappears his stance becomes unsettled. The world never stays the same:
We alternate among people these days
Someone who turns to Allah, however, finds the foundation of reassurance in the One who does not die, obeying His words:
Put your trust in the Ever-Living Who never dies
The Prophet’s bedtime supplication expresses this reliance in the words
I have sought shelter for my back with You
. Reliance is not simply a subject to discuss while leaving our fears and hopes untouched; it means bringing our worries to our Lord while trusting Him.
In saying
O Allah! Thou art Peace, and peace comes from Thee
, a person remembers that the reassurance he seeks is not limited to an improvement in some passing circumstance: he asks his Lord for it.
Knowing Allah’s beautiful names therefore requires living with their meanings, rather than simply memorizing definitions.
Someone reading Joseph’s story sees Allah’s gentle care for him throughout its events. The name al-Latif then touches him in a way that a lifeless expression detached from life does not.
He may hear of Allah’s self-sufficiency and generosity, then experience a need that turns him to Him, discovering the effect of that name on his heart in a way he did not when he merely heard it.

Frequent exposure to great truths, however, can become a habit that weakens our response. Someone visiting a sick person may feel his heart soften and remember the blessing of health, while some hospital workers grow familiar with repeated scenes of illness and death and need to renew the lessons they draw from them. Someone arriving at the Sacred Sanctuary may long for it and weep on reaching it, while some who work there regularly need to struggle against familiarity so that it does not veil the greatness of the place.
The point concerns the effect of familiarity; it is not a judgment on a profession or on the hearts of those who work in it.

Likewise, someone who spends a long time discussing Allah in the abstract, yet experiences little humility or sense of need before Him, needs to return to the Quran and receive what it says about his Lord, rather than be content with analyzing words. His Creator knows best what will speak to his heart:
Does He not know His Own creation[1], when He is the Most Subtle, the All-Aware?
One supplication that brings together calling on Allah by His names and benefiting from His words asks Him
to make the Quran the springtime of my heart, the light of my chest, the clearing of my sorrow, and the removal of my worry
This orientation does not become firmly established through listening to an admonition alone. Action plants in the heart a regard for what a person works for.

People do not need a lesson every morning to remind them of the value of their worldly affairs. Their daily involvement, the effort they spend acquiring what they want, and the time they devote to it all strengthen their attachment.
Likewise, someone who makes an effort to maintain prayer, sets aside time for remembrance and supplication, and labors to learn and teach others will grow in reverence for what he devotes himself to.
Hearing about sincere devotion or sharing words about it, while changing nothing in one’s actions, cannot take the place of striving to reform the heart. Praise and reward are connected to action:
How excellent is the reward of those who do [righteous] deeds!

Moving from scattered desires to reassurance in Allah is therefore a repeated effort: knowledge followed by worship, and worship through which that knowledge takes effect afresh. This keeps the words from remaining merely a definition explained by the tongue:
Allah, the Eternal Refuge[1].
They become a truth to which the heart returns in its needs, fears, efforts, and choices.

publisherNotes.text: [1] He is absolute, perfect, complete, self-sufficient; the one eternally and constantly required and sought; all existence depend upon Him; all matters ultimately return to Him.
[2] The path of Truth and Justice, as He Almighty does not deal anyone wrongfully.
[1] i.e., they do not worship others besides Allah.
[1] Before Whom nothing existed; the foremost; the uppermost.
[1] i.e., with uncertainty, hypocrisy, or heedlessness.
[2] lit., they tumble on their faces, i.e., turn back to disbelief.
[1] Or does He not know those whom He created?
